metaDescription: Six label printers for MRP work, covering maximum-retail-price pack stickers and manufacturing batch, lot and bin labels, with the data fields each handles.
expertTake: The SUPVAN T50M Pro is the pick for small producers who print price, batch and date on pack stickers from an app, because its wide waterproof labels hold up in a chilled or damp stockroom. The Rollo USB is the value-minded choice for work-order and shipment labels from a computer. Anyone who needs regulated pack labelling should check the legal format before choosing any printer.
introParagraphs: MRP means two different things in two different workplaces. In retail packaging it is the maximum retail price stamped on a pack, often with a batch number and a date. In a factory it is material requirements planning, where labels carry lot, bin and work-order data. Both are variable-data jobs, and the printer matters less than how easily it changes a field.

That shapes the shopping list. A good MRP printer lets a user change one number and print twenty copies without redesigning the label, takes a label size that fits the pack or the bin, and keeps the print readable through handling. This guide ranks six printers on those practical points.

products.name: SUPVAN T50M Pro Bluetooth label maker, 3/4 to 2 in

specList.label: Editing
specList.value: App on phone, tablet or PC

products.description:
For a small producer printing price, batch and date on pack stickers, the T50M Pro covers the essential needs in a light body. It prints labels from 3/4 to 2 inches wide, which fits jars, pouches and small cartons, and the listing says the label material is waterproof. A chilled or damp stockroom is the sort of place where plain paper stickers curl and smear.

The app runs on a phone, tablet or PC and offers more than 30 fonts and image import, so a logo, a price line and a batch code can sit on one label. Variable data is the weak point of every phone-driven printer, since changing a date for each batch means reopening the label. Against the Nelko P21, it prints wider labels, which helps when the price needs to be large.

Keep spare tapes, wipe the head and save a template per product. A good practice is to keep the template's batch and date fields in the same position on every product, so a packer learns where to look and an inspector can check quickly. Print the first sticker of each batch and compare it with the batch sheet before the rest, since a wrong date repeated fifty times is a costly mistake.
products.bestFor: Small producers who print price, batch and date stickers from an app.
pros: App on phone, tablet and PC
cons: Changing batch data means editing the label

products.name: Rollo USB 4x6 direct thermal printer

specList.label: Computer support
specList.value: Windows XP and newer, Mac 10.9 and newer

products.description:
In a factory, MRP output often means a big label that travels with a batch: a work order, a lot number, a bin location. The Rollo USB prints that on 4x6 direct thermal labels from any Windows or Mac computer, with a driver list that goes back to Windows XP and Mac 10.9. That reach matters on a shop floor where the computer attached to the printer may be a decade old.

It prints whatever the planning software sends it, so the quality of the label depends on the template in that software, not on the printer. There is no phone route and no built-in design tool beyond the shipping app. Against the wireless Rollo, it is wired and steadier, with no network to maintain.

Use direct thermal labels meant for a few weeks, and wipe the head every few rolls. In a plant, the planning software usually decides the label layout, so spend your effort on the template and test it with a few real orders. An old computer attached to the printer can keep working for years if you avoid updating its operating system, a point worth discussing with whoever manages your systems.
products.bestFor: Plants that print lot and work-order labels from an old Windows computer.
pros: Driver support reaches back to old systems
4x6 size suits work orders and lot tags
cons: Direct thermal prints fade over months

products.name: Rollo Wireless Wi-Fi 4x6 label printer
products.description:
The wireless Rollo suits a floor where several people print batch labels from tablets or laptops. It joins the Wi-Fi network, accepts AirPrint from Apple devices and prints at 150 millimeters per second, so a supervisor can send a lot label from a tablet while walking the line.

Its weakness is the network. A metal-heavy factory is rough on Wi-Fi, and a dropped link at shift change is a real cost. Compared with the wired Rollo, you gain placement freedom and lose steadiness. It prints the same label, so the choice is about where the printer must sit.

Mount it where the signal is strong, give it a fixed address and keep a USB-connected backup printer if the line cannot stop. A quick check at the start of each shift, printing one label from the tablet, shows whether the network is healthy before the rush begins. If the signal is marginal, move the printer or add an access point rather than blaming the machine.
products.bestFor: Floors where several supervisors print lot labels from tablets.
pros: Wi-Fi with AirPrint for Apple devices
Same 4x6 label as the wired model

products.name: KNAON 4x6 Bluetooth thermal label printer, white

specList.label: Wired
specList.value: USB for macOS, Windows 7 and up, ChromeOS

products.description:
KNAON pairs Bluetooth with USB, which gives a production planner two ways to reach the same label printer. A phone can print a quick bin label while the planner walks the stockroom, and a computer on USB handles the bulk. The listing also mentions a template library that helps with non-standard labels.

The template library is handy for pre-set MRP layouts where only a number changes. It does not state a database or batch feature, so the variable-data work still happens in your planning software or in the app. Against the Rollo USB, it adds mobility and ChromeOS support.

Keep the cable beside it, re-pair after phone updates and wipe the head regularly. A planner who prints bin labels at the shelf should carry a few pre-printed spares of the commonest codes, because a label printed in advance beats a pairing glitch in a cold store. Use a stock that is rated for the temperature of the room where it will live.
products.bestFor: Planners who print from both a phone and a computer.
cons: No batch or database feature stated

products.name: Nelko P21 Bluetooth label printer, black

specList.label: Phones
specList.value: iOS and Android through the Nelko app

specList.label: Weight
specList.value: About half the weight and size of traditional label makers

products.description:
For a one-person kitchen or a stall that needs a price and a date on a small pack, the P21 is the lightest answer here. The listing calls it half the weight and size of traditional label makers, and it pairs with iOS and Android phones through the Nelko app. Templates mean a price label can be made in a minute.

Its prints are direct thermal and fade, so it suits short-life stickers on packs that sell within days. It has no database feature, so each batch needs the number edited by hand. Next to the T50M Pro, it prints narrower stickers.

Store a spare roll in the same pouch and update the app now and then. Because the stickers fade, date the roll when you open it and use the oldest first. A pack that sits for months should carry a label printed near the time it was made, and a label that has gone pale reads poorly to a customer.
products.bestFor: Home producers who print price and date stickers on small packs.
pros: About half the weight of traditional machines

products.name: DYMO LetraTag 100H handheld label maker

specList.label: Tape finishes
specList.value: Paper, clear, opaque plastic and textile

products.description:
DYMO's LetraTag 100H is the simple tape option for bin tags and shelf edges. It is a slim, lightweight handheld that prints on 12 millimeter LetraTag tapes in paper, clear, opaque plastic and textile finishes. For a stockroom that needs a quick part number or lot code on a bin, that is all that is needed.

It has no app and no database, so each label is typed by hand. That is a strength for a handful of tags and a weakness for a long run of numbered labels. The textile finish is interesting for labeling fabric goods or workwear, a use the thermal printers cannot match.

Keep spare tape cassettes, replace batteries before a long run and clean the cutter occasionally.
products.bestFor: Stockrooms that need quick hand-typed bin and shelf tags.
pros: Paper, clear, plastic and textile tape finishes
12 mm tape suits bin and shelf edges
cons: Hand typing is slow for long numbered runs

buyingCriteria.explanation: A retail pack carrying a maximum retail price needs a sticker sized to the pack, with the price legible and often a batch and date alongside. A manufacturing plan needs lot, bin and order labels at a larger size. The SUPVAN T50M Pro and Nelko P21 suit the first job, and the Rollo and KNAON printers suit the second. Name the job before choosing the printer. Teams often discover mid-project that their pack labels also need a work-order sheet, and a second printer enters the budget. Listing every label you print in a normal week, with its size and who prints it, is the quickest way to see whether one machine or two will do.

MRP labels are mostly the same label with one field changed: a batch number, a date or a lot. Phone apps handle this by editing and reprinting, which is slow for long runs. Planning software on a computer, driving the Rollo USB, can print a whole sequence from a list. If you change data often, favor the computer route. A spreadsheet or planning screen that holds the batch numbers can drive a printer through its normal driver, so the printer itself only needs to take a standard label. Where no computer exists on the floor, accept that each batch needs a manual edit and build that step into the routine.

On a small pack, the price and date must be readable at a glance. The T50M Pro prints up to 2 inch wide labels and the Nelko P21 prints narrower ones. A wider label allows a larger font. Print a test sticker at the final size and read it from arm's length, since cramped type is the most common failure.

Packs get handled, chilled and wetted. The T50M Pro states waterproof labels, and the DYMO LetraTag 100H offers plastic and textile tape. Direct thermal paper labels from the Rollo, KNAON and Nelko fade with heat and age. Match the label material to the pack's life and storage.

Where a law prescribes the content or placement of a price or date on a pack, a printer cannot make a label compliant on its own. Check the rule for your product and region, and design the label accordingly. A printer that prints crisp characters helps, but compliance lives in the template.

The Rollo printers need a computer or tablet, the KNAON works with either, the SUPVAN and Nelko work from a phone, and the DYMO LetraTag works alone. A producer with no computer on the floor will not use a USB printer. Choose the route your people will actually use. The best printer on paper is wasted if the person on the night shift has to ask for help. Ask the people who will print what device they carry and what they are comfortable with, then choose to suit them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to the MRP job
howWeEvaluated.description: We sorted printers into pack-sticker and work-order classes. The SUPVAN and Nelko suit pack stickers, the Rollo and KNAON suit work orders, and the DYMO suits bin tags. This sorting shaped the whole ranking.

howWeEvaluated.title: Variable data handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We asked how easily each printer prints a changing field. Computer-driven printers handle sequences best. App-driven printers need manual editing. None of the listings states a database feature.

howWeEvaluated.title: Label legibility and size
howWeEvaluated.description: Maximum widths were compared: 3/4 to 2 inches for the SUPVAN, 4x6 for the Rollo and KNAON, and 12 millimeters for the DYMO. Larger labels give more room for legible price and date lines.

howWeEvaluated.title: Survival of the label
howWeEvaluated.description: Waterproof, plastic and textile materials were compared with plain direct thermal paper. The SUPVAN and DYMO score for survival. The thermal paper printers score lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Operator fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered whether staff will use the route offered: computer, phone or standalone. A printer nobody can operate is no use, however good its specs.

maintenance.why: Variable-data labels repeat. A template means only the batch field changes.
Lint and adhesive cause pale text on a price line. Alcohol on a swab clears them.

A weak battery on the handheld produces faint characters.
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth settings can reset after updates.

faq.q: What does MRP mean for label printing?
faq.a: It can mean maximum retail price stickers on packs or material requirements planning labels with lot and bin data. Choose a printer for whichever you do, and write the job down before you shop, since a pack sticker and a work-order label call for very different machines.

faq.q: Can these printers print a batch number automatically?
faq.a: None of the listings advertises it. Sequences usually come from planning software on a computer driving a 4x6 printer.

faq.q: Which printer suits retail pack stickers?
faq.a: The SUPVAN T50M Pro, because of its wide waterproof labels. The Nelko P21 suits smaller packs.

faq.q: Do labels need to be waterproof?
faq.a: For chilled or damp stock, yes. For dry shelves, ordinary thermal paper is fine.

faq.q: Does a printer make a label legally compliant?
faq.a: No. Compliance depends on the content and placement of the label. Check the rules for your product.

faq.q: Which is easiest for a team without computers?
faq.a: The DYMO LetraTag 100H prints alone. The SUPVAN and Nelko work from a phone.
